title: What Happens to Your Body When You Exercise?
paragraphs: The moment you begin to exercise, a coordinated set of adjustments is set in motion. Heart rate and breathing accelerate to deliver more oxygen, blood vessels in the active muscles dilate, and blood is diverted away from organs whose work can wait, such as the stomach and intestines.

Inside the muscle cells, oxygen and fuel, chiefly glucose and fatty acids, are converted into the energy molecules that power contraction. This conversion is far from efficient: a large share of the energy escapes as heat, raising core temperature and prompting the body to sweat. During very intense effort, muscles increasingly draw on anaerobic pathways, which provide rapid energy but cannot be sustained for long.

The effects on the brain are equally significant. Exercise boosts cerebral blood flow and stimulates the release of neurochemicals associated with improved mood and resilience to stress. A substantial body of research has linked regular physical activity to better sleep quality, enhanced cognitive function and a reduced risk of depression and dementia.

Sustained training produces lasting adaptations: the heart pumps more blood per beat, resting heart rate typically declines, and muscles, bones and tendons become stronger. The World Health Organization recommends that adults accumulate 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, each week, together with muscle-strengthening exercise at least twice a week.
